analysis.one_liner: Makes pharmacy benefit managers legally accountable to employer health plans as fiduciaries.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2025 with bipartisan support and referred to the Senate health committee, where it awaits action.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are middlemen that employer health plans hire to negotiate drug prices, build the lists of covered drugs, and pay pharmacy claims. This bill amends the federal law governing employer health plans (ERISA) to treat PBMs as fiduciaries, meaning they would be legally required to put the health plan's interests ahead of their own profits, and to disclose all the compensation they receive from drug makers and others. It also bars PBMs from writing contracts that excuse them from liability if they breach those duties. The bill has been referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families covered by employer health plans, who pay part of their drug costs out of pocket and whose premiums reflect what the plan pays for drugs. Employers who sponsor plans also gain, because they would have clearer legal recourse against PBMs that profit at the plan's expense.

how_it_helps.text: Deems PBMs to be fiduciaries under ERISA when they maintain drug networks or formularies, negotiate rebates, process claims, or conduct utilization review for a group health plan, legally binding them to act in the plan's interest rather than their own.

Requires PBMs and third-party administrators to disclose direct and indirect compensation they expect to receive, including money tied to building drug networks and purchasing drugs from manufacturers, wholesalers, rebate aggregators, and group purchasing organizations.
Prohibits PBMs from being indemnified or otherwise relieved from liability for breaches of these fiduciary duties, and voids any contract provision that tries to do so.

Clarifies that a PBM or other service provider cannot serve as the 'responsible plan fiduciary' overseeing the required fee disclosures, preventing the party being paid from policing its own compensation.

analysis.who_pays: PBMs and their parent companies, which are often owned by large insurance conglomerates, would face new legal liability, disclosure obligations, and exposure to lawsuits if they profit at a health plan's expense. The cost would come out of industry margins; plans might also see some administrative costs from compliance.

drawbacks.text: Making PBMs fiduciaries could expose them to substantial litigation risk, and some of that cost could be passed back to health plans and employers through higher fees.

Fiduciary status and disclosure rules address conduct but do not directly cap drug prices or PBMs' spreads; critics of PBM reform legislation more broadly argue that narrower structural fixes, such as delinking PBM pay from drug list prices, go further. This bill's focus is accountability, not pricing.
The bill covers group health plans under ERISA, so it does not reach government plans, individual market coverage, or other arrangements outside that framework.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefits go to workers and employers with ERISA health plans, in the form of stronger legal accountability and fee transparency from the middlemen who shape what they pay for prescription drugs. The cost falls mainly on PBM companies, with some risk of higher administrative fees passed to plans. The bill does not by itself lower drug prices, but it strengthens the legal position of the people and employers who pay them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was just introduced in December 2025 and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, where it has not yet received a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill on December 17, 2025, joined by Sens. Tim Kaine (D), Chuck Grassley (R), and Maggie Hassan (D).
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; no further action has been taken.

The bill would amend ERISA to deem PBMs fiduciaries, require disclosure of their compensation from drug makers and related third parties, bar indemnification for fiduciary breaches, and prevent a service provider from serving as the fiduciary overseeing its own fee disclosures.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PBMs are better off so far: the bill has not advanced past committee referral, so the current legal rules allowing them to profit without fiduciary accountability remain in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PBMs, while the bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PBM FAIR Act in the Senate on December 17, 2025.

for.name: Sens. Tim Kaine, Chuck Grassley, and Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a mixed-party roster of four Senate backers (two Republicans, two Democrats) and no recorded opposition yet, since no committee or floor action has occurred.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (often owned by large insurers)
industries.note: PBMs profit on drug pricing spreads, rebate arrangements, and administrative fees; the bill makes them fiduciaries with disclosure duties and new liability exposure if they put their own profit ahead of the plans they serve. That is precisely the conduct the bill targets.
Employers would gain clearer legal recourse and fee transparency from their PBM contractors, and the bill notes PBMs can still serve as fiduciary for their own employee plans.

Their rebate and discount arrangements would be disclosed under the bill's compensation rules, increasing scrutiny of how much of negotiated savings reaches health plans, though the bill does not directly cap their prices.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate HELP Committee with bipartisan sponsorship but no hearing, markup, or floor action. Most bills at this stage in a two-year Congress never advance; its prospects depend on the committee leadership choosing to take up PBM legislation, a topic that has drawn periodic bipartisan interest but has not produced a stand-alone law.
